title: Projected US Job Displacement from AI by 2030
description: Projected net percentage of US jobs displaced by AI and automation by 2030, synthesizing displacement estimates, observed employment data, and net-of-job-creation projections.

proxyContext.actualUnit: relative job posting decline per SD of GenAI exposure
proxyContext.rationale: 8% relative posting decline (1-SD exposure) converted via 0.30 factor; postings overstate displacement ~2-3x

proxyContext.actualUnit: percentage point decline in employment-to-population ratio
proxyContext.rationale: EPOP decline used as direct proxy for job displacement percentage

proxyContext.actualUnit: percentage point drop in AI-exposed occupation employment share
proxyContext.rationale: 16.4% to 15.5% employment share decline in AI-exposed occupations used as displacement proxy

proxyContext.actualUnit: % net headcount decline in 5 AI-exposed sectors globally
proxyContext.rationale: Global survey of 935 execs across 5 sectors (consumer staples, real estate, transport, healthcare equip, autos); US showed +2% net gain, UK -8%, Germany -4%, auto sector -10%

proxyContext.actualUnit: LFPR decline attributable to AI in rapid progress scenario
proxyContext.rationale: Economists forecast LFPR drop from 62.6% to 59.1% by 2030 in rapid AI scenario, with ~half (~1.75pp, ~10M jobs) attributable to AI. 10M/166M labor force ≈ 6%. CONDITIONAL on rapid scenario which economists assign only 14% probability. Probability-weighted expected displacement ≈ 0.8%.

proxyContext.actualUnit: % of US jobs at higher short-term automation risk (framework category)
proxyContext.rationale: OpenAI's framework classifies 18% of 921 occupations (147.9M jobs) as facing higher short-term automation risk — high exposure, weak human necessity, limited demand offset. Authors explicitly caveat that categories are NOT forecasts of direct job loss; this is an upper-bound risk share, hence proxy discount.

sources.title: The History of Technological Anxiety and the Future of Economic Growth: Is This Time Different?
sources.publisher: Journal of Economic Perspectives (Mokyr, Vickers, Ziebarth)
sources.excerpt: The evidence is that technological unemployment did not occur on a large scale during the Industrial Revolution. The fears of the Luddites that machinery would impoverish workers were not realized, and the main reason is well understood: mechanization could only replace a limited number of human activities, while technological change increased the demand for other types of labor that were complementary to the capital goods embodied in the new technologies.

sources.title: AI and Jobs: The Role of Demand
sources.excerpt: If demand is sufficiently elastic and AI does not completely replace humans, then technical change will create jobs rather than destroy them. In manufacturing, technology sharply reduced jobs in recent decades. But before that, for over a century, employment grew, even in industries experiencing rapid technological change. What changed? Demand was highly elastic at first and then became inelastic.

sources.title: Automation and jobs: when technology boosts employment
sources.excerpt: The main impact of automation in the near future may be to cause a major reallocation of jobs, even if it does not permanently eliminate large numbers of jobs. During the 19th century, technologies had automated 98% of the labour required to weave a yard of cloth. Yet, the number of weaving jobs actually increased for decades over this period.

sources.title: The Potentially Large Effects of AI on Economic Growth
sources.excerpt: Roughly two-thirds of current jobs are exposed to some degree of AI automation; generative AI could substitute up to one-fourth of current work.

sources.title: OECD Employment Outlook 2023: AI and the Labour Market
sources.excerpt: 27% of jobs are in occupations at high risk of automation across OECD countries.

sources.title: Gen-AI: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work
sources.excerpt: Almost 40% of global employment is exposed to AI, with advanced economies more affected.

sources.title: AI Is Starting to Threaten White-Collar Jobs. Few Industries Are Immune.
sources.excerpt: White-collar layoffs growing as companies link cuts to AI. Google, Duolingo, UPS all reduced workforce. Nearly two-thirds of white-collar workers report improved productivity from AI use.

sources.title: The Simple Macroeconomics of AI
sources.excerpt: AI may increase TFP by only 0.53-0.66% over 10 years under the most aggressive assumptions. Only about 4.6% of all tasks will be affected by AI, and cost savings on these tasks are modest (averaging 27%). The implied GDP effect is 0.93-1.16% over a decade — far below popular estimates. The displacement effect on jobs is correspondingly small, well under 1% of employment.

sources.title: AI Adoption and Employment-to-Population Ratio
sources.excerpt: AI adoption associated with -0.6 percentage point decline in employment-to-population ratio.

sources.title: Geographic Vulnerability to AI Displacement
sources.excerpt: High-education, high-cost metros are most vulnerable to AI displacement.

sources.title: GenAI and STEM Entrepreneurship
sources.excerpt: GenAI increased STEM incorporated entrepreneurship; displacement may be offset by new firm creation.

sources.title: Forrester: AI And Automation Job Impact Forecast
sources.excerpt: AI and automation could account for 6% of total US job losses by 2030, equating to 10.4 million roles. Widespread AI-driven job replacement remains unlikely. AI will augment 20% of jobs rather than eliminate them.

sources.title: Elevating Human Potential: The AI Skills Revolution
sources.excerpt: Among respondents actively using or experimenting with AI, 93% agree that it allows them to focus more on higher-level responsibilities. The leading response (53%) was 'AI will augment human capabilities, leading to increased productivity and new forms of innovation.'

sources.title: Displacement or Complementarity? The Labor Market Impact of Generative AI
sources.excerpt: 17% decrease in job postings for highly automatable occupations, but 22% increase for augmentation-prone ones — net effect depends on occupation mix.

sources.title: Total US Job Postings Trend Analysis — January 2025
sources.excerpt: Total US job postings are 15% below their February 2022 peak. Categories most exposed to AI (data entry, basic admin, customer service) show steepest declines.

sources.title: AI exposure predicts unemployment risk
sources.excerpt: Workers in AI-exposed occupations face significantly higher unemployment risk.

sources.title: Automatic Reaction — What Happens to Workers at Firms that Automate?
sources.publisher: Review of Economics and Statistics (Bessen, Goos, Salomons, van den Berge)
sources.excerpt: Only 0.7% of all workers on average leave their employers each year due to automation. The risk of losing a job due to automation is much smaller than the risk of a mass layoff (3.5-7.2%/yr in the Netherlands).

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Labor Market
sources.excerpt: Most adversely impacted occupations (business, financial, engineering) experienced a decline of 2% to 2.5% over a five-year period. Reduced demand in exposed occupations is offset by productivity-driven increases in labor demand at AI-adopting firms.

sources.title: Incorporating AI impacts in BLS employment projections: occupational case studies

sources.title: Displacement or Complementarity? The Labor Market Impact of Generative AI
sources.excerpt: 24% decrease in generative AI-exposed skills per firm per quarter in top-quartile automation-exposed jobs. 15% increase in AI-exposed skills for augmentation-prone jobs. Augmentation-prone job postings increased 22% per quarter per firm.

sources.title: Steering Technological Progress
sources.excerpt: Framework for guiding innovation to increase labor demand; steering technology becomes more desirable the less efficient social safety nets are.

sources.title: We're not ready for mass AI unemployment
Displacement or Complementarity? The Labor Market Impact of Generative AI
sources.excerpt: Using O*NET and LightCast job postings data (2019-June 2024), the study found a 24% decrease in generative AI-exposed skills per firm per quarter for automation-prone occupations, while augmentation-prone occupations saw a 15% increase. Demonstrates the dual displacement/complementarity impact of generative AI.

sources.title: Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects
sources.excerpt: Workplaces that adopted AI chatbots showed no significant difference in employment, early-career jobs, job churn, or worker mix. Difference-in-differences estimates for earnings and wages are all precisely estimated zeros, ruling out effects larger than 2%.

sources.title: AI, Productivity, and Technological Unemployment
sources.excerpt: Calibrated to U.S. data, the model predicts more than threefold productivity improvements alongside a long-run employment loss of 23%, with half (~11.5%) occurring over the initial five-year transition period.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence and Technological Unemployment
sources.publisher: NBER / Richmond Fed (Ping Wang, Tsz-Nga Wong)
sources.excerpt: Calibrated to U.S. data, the model predicts more than threefold improvements in productivity in the some-AI steady state, alongside a long-run employment loss of 23%, with half this loss occurring over the initial five-year transition.

sources.title: A Quarter of Companies in Germany Expect Job Cuts Due to Artificial Intelligence
sources.excerpt: 27.1% of companies expect artificial intelligence to lead to job cuts in the next five years. Only 5.2% of companies anticipate additional jobs, while two-thirds expect no change.

sources.title: PwC 2025 Global AI Jobs Barometer
sources.excerpt: Job numbers are growing in every industry analysed. Growth remained robust even in more exposed occupations (38%). Productivity growth nearly quadrupled in AI-exposed industries.

sources.title: Amazon deploys its 1 millionth robot in a sign of more job automation
sources.excerpt: Amazon deployed its 1 millionth robot across over 300 fulfillment centers worldwide. CEO Andy Jassy acknowledged that AI will result in fewer people doing some automated jobs, while new roles in robotics maintenance grew 30% at next-generation sites.

sources.title: Bureau of Labor Statistics Employment Projections 2024-2034
How Will AI Affect the Global Workforce?

sources.title: Is AI Contributing to Rising Unemployment? Evidence from Occupational Variation
sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
sources.excerpt: Occupations with higher AI exposure experienced larger unemployment rate increases between 2022 and 2025 (r=0.47). Computer/math occupations (exposure ~80%) saw steepest rises. GenAI-intensive occupations: r=0.57.

sources.title: Yes, AI Is Affecting Employment. Here's the Data
sources.excerpt: In jobs with high AI exposure, employment for 22- to 25-year-olds fell 6% between late 2022 and July 2025. Software developers saw a 20% early-career decline. Employment among workers 30 and older grew 6-13%.

sources.title: AI's Use of Knowledge in Society
sources.excerpt: In the absence of active countermeasures, transformative AI may lead to significantly more centralization of decision-making. Some types of information might defy codification, and some types of information processing might be better done locally.

sources.title: Job Transformation, Specialization, and the Labor Market Effects of AI
sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis (Freund, Mann)
sources.excerpt: Within highly exposed occupations, like office and administrative roles, workers specialized in information-processing tasks leave and suffer wage losses, while those specialized in customer-facing and coordination tasks stay and experience wage gains as work rebalances toward their strengths.

sources.title: The Projected Impact of Generative AI on Future Productivity Growth
sources.excerpt: Roughly 10% of US work affected in the short run; AI will increase productivity and GDP by 1.5% by 2035. Jobs that AI can completely replace saw 0.75% employment fall 2021-2024.

sources.title: AI and jobs: A review of theory, estimates, and evidence
sources.excerpt: Productivity gains 20-60% in controlled RCTs, 15-30% in field experiments; AI exposure measures converge toward high-wage jobs being most exposed.

sources.title: AI Labor Market Impact: Freelancers
sources.excerpt: More than half of businesses using freelancers in 2022 have stopped entirely; freelance marketplace spend fell from 0.66% to 0.14% of total business spend.

sources.title: New data show no AI jobs apocalypse — for now
sources.excerpt: Despite fears of imminent AI jobs apocalypse, the overall labor market shows more continuity than disruption since ChatGPT's launch.

sources.title: AI and the U.S. Labor Market: No Macro Displacement Yet
sources.excerpt: Analysis finds no significant macro-level job displacement from AI as of late 2025, though structural shifts are emerging in specific sectors.

sources.title: Remote Labor Index: Measuring AI Automation of Remote Work
sources.publisher: Center for AI Safety / Scale AI (Mazeika et al.)
sources.excerpt: AI agents perform near the floor on RLI, with the highest-performing agent achieving an automation rate of 2.5%. 240 real freelance projects across game dev, design, architecture, data analysis, and animation. Best agent earned $1,720 of $143,991 total project value.

sources.title: Labor Demand in the Age of Generative AI: Early Evidence from the U.S. Job Posting Data
sources.excerpt: Job postings for high-AI-substitution occupations fell 12% relative to low-substitution roles post-ChatGPT. Effect grew from 6% in year one to 18% by year three. This measures posting-level demand shifts, not direct employment changes.

sources.title: The Adoption of ChatGPT
sources.excerpt: Study of 11 occupations in Denmark: essentially zero effects on earnings and hours worked; confidence intervals rule out effects larger than 2%. AI adoption linked to ~4% occupational switching.

sources.title: McKinsey Global Survey on AI (State of AI, 2025)

sources.title: Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of AI
sources.publisher: Stanford Digital Economy Lab (Brynjolfsson, Chandar, Chen)
sources.excerpt: Overall employment continues to grow robustly, but employment growth for young workers has been stagnant since late 2022. Declining employment in AI-exposed jobs drives stagnant overall employment growth for 22- to 25-year-olds.

sources.title: Agents, robots, and us: Skill partnerships in the age of AI
sources.publisher: McKinsey Global Institute (Yee, Madgavkar, Smit et al.)
sources.excerpt: Currently demonstrated technologies could automate activities accounting for about 57 percent of US work hours today. AI agents could perform tasks occupying 44 percent of US work hours, while robots could handle another 13 percent. Roles with the highest potential for automation make up about 40 percent of total jobs.

sources.title: The Iceberg Index: Measuring Skills-centered Exposure in the AI Economy
sources.excerpt: AI can already replace 11.7% of the U.S. workforce, or as much as $1.2 trillion in wages across finance, health care, and professional services. The visible tip — tech sector layoffs — represents just 2.2% of total wage exposure ($211B). Simulated 151 million workers across 32,000 skills and 3,000 counties.

sources.title: Future of Jobs Report 2025
sources.excerpt: 40% of employers globally expect to reduce headcount as AI automates tasks. Net displacement estimates range from 5-14% of current roles by 2030.

sources.title: Unwilling to Reskill? Experimental Evidence from Real-World Jobseekers
sources.excerpt: Perceived 'identity fit' — whether a new skill feels compatible with a person's sense of self — dominated re-skilling decisions, often outweighing beliefs about wages or employer demand.

sources.title: The Labor Market Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence
sources.publisher: Stanford / World Bank (Hartley, Jolevski, Melo, Moore)
sources.excerpt: 35.9% of US workers used generative AI by December 2025; small positive wage effects, no significant decline in job openings.

sources.title: AI Adoption and Employment in EU Firms
sources.excerpt: EU firms see +4% productivity from AI adoption; no employment decline detected.

sources.title: O-Ring Automation
sources.excerpt: Task-by-task substitution logic is incomplete because automating one task changes the return to automating others. Automation decisions are discrete and can require bundled adoption even when automation quality improves smoothly.

sources.title: Young workers' employment drops in occupations with high AI exposure
sources.excerpt: If fully translated to unemployment, AI-driven employment declines among young workers would explain only 0.1 percentage point rise in aggregate unemployment.

sources.title: Young workers' employment drops in occupations with high AI exposure
sources.excerpt: Employment share for AI-exposed occupations fell from 16.4% (Nov 2022) to 15.5% (Sep 2025). Workers age 22-25 in most AI-exposed occupations experienced 13% employment decline since 2022, driven by fewer workforce entrants rather than layoffs.

sources.title: Can advanced AI lead to negative economic growth?
sources.excerpt: automation can depress demand and push AI-driven growth toward the lower end of current forecasts. [...] the conditions needed for growth to actually turn negative are likely too unrealistic to hold in practice

sources.title: Past Automation and Future A.I.: How Weak Links Tame the Growth Explosion

sources.title: How Adaptable Are American Workers to AI-Induced Job Displacement?
sources.excerpt: Of the 37.1 million workers in the top quartile of AI exposure, 26.5 million are in occupations that also have above-median adaptive capacity. At the same time, 6.1 million workers (4.2% of the workforce) are both highly exposed and in the bottom quartile of adaptive capacity, concentrated in clerical and administrative roles.

sources.title: January 2026 US Labor Market Update: Jobs Mentioning AI Are Growing Amid Broader Hiring Weakness
sources.excerpt: the Indeed Job Postings Index, which was down 5.2% year-over-year as of December 31

sources.title: Dalende werkgelegenheid onder Nederlandse jongeren die concurreren met GenAI
sources.excerpt: In het derde kwartaal van 2025 werkten ruim dertien procent minder jongeren in de meest vatbare beroepsgroepen dan in het vierde kwartaal van 2022, terwijl de werkgelegenheid in andere beroepsgroepen juist drie procent steeg.

sources.title: AI, Productivity, and Labor Markets: A Review of the Empirical Evidence
sources.excerpt: No measurable change in job openings or aggregate employment in AI-exposed occupations; adjustment happening through task reallocation, not broad displacement.

sources.title: Minimum Wages and Rise of the Robots
sources.excerpt: a 10 percent increase in the minimum wage increases robot adoption by roughly 8 percent relative to the mean

sources.title: Firm Data on AI
sources.excerpt: Synthesizes firm-level survey data from the US, UK, Germany, and Australia measuring AI's realized and expected impacts on sales per employee and employment. Data collected Feb-Apr 2025 and Nov 2025-Jan 2026.

sources.title: FRED JOLTS: Job Openings Total Nonfarm — February 2026
sources.excerpt: Job openings at 6,882K in February 2026, gradual decline from 2024 peaks.

sources.title: Job Openings and Labor Turnover — December 2025
sources.excerpt: Job openings fell to their lowest level since December 2017. Quits rate held steady at 2%, remaining below its 2019 average.

sources.title: AI's Impact Accelerates: AlphaWise Survey of 935 Executives
sources.excerpt: Survey respondents said that AI adoption had led to elimination of 11% of jobs and an additional 12% were left unfilled. This is partially offset by 18% new hires, resulting in a 4% net job loss globally.

sources.title: Firm Data on AI
sources.excerpt: Survey of ~6,000 executives across US, UK, Germany, Australia. 90%+ report no employment impact from AI over the past 3 years. Firms expect AI to reduce employment by 0.7% over the next 3 years (US: -1.2%). Employees, by contrast, expect +0.5% job creation.

sources.title: How AI is affecting productivity and jobs in Europe
sources.publisher: CEPR VoxEU (Aldasoro, Gambacorta, Pál, Revoltella, Weiss, Wolski)
sources.excerpt: No evidence that AI reduces employment in the short run. AI augments worker output — enabling employees to complete tasks faster and make better decisions — without displacing labour.

sources.title: AI and the US Labor Market: Current Impact and Outlook
sources.excerpt: AI's labor market impact still small — only 5-10K/month drag on net job growth. Only 2½% of jobs exposed to automation today. Baseline forecast: 6-7% of workers displaced (range 3-14%), lowering annual hiring by 1M jobs and raising unemployment ~½pp. US creates 30M gross new jobs/year; does not anticipate job apocalypse. Impact so far largely confined to tech sector but expects it to grow materially.

sources.title: AI is simultaneously aiding and replacing workers, wage data suggest
sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas (J. Scott Davis)
sources.excerpt: employment has declined 1 percent since late 2022 in the 10 percent of sectors most exposed to AI

sources.title: How Well Does Agent Development Reflect Real-World Work?
sources.excerpt: We first analyze 43 benchmarks and 72,342 tasks, measuring their alignment with human employment and capital allocation across all 1,016 real-world occupations in the U.S. labor market.

sources.title: Mind the Gap: AI Adoption in Europe and the U.S.
sources.excerpt: We do not find clear evidence that industry-level AI adoption is associated with employment changes.

sources.title: FRED Unemployment Level — March 2026
sources.excerpt: Unemployment level 7,239K in March 2026.

sources.title: Steering Technological Progress
sources.excerpt: As technology devalues labor, optimal policy shifts from steering innovation toward redistribution.

sources.title: US Economics Analyst: Earnings Season Takeaways: AI-nxiety
sources.excerpt: While we still do not find a meaningful relationship between productivity and AI adoption at the economywide level, companies that quantified productivity impacts of AI on specific tasks reported a median productivity gain of around 30%.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence: friend or foe for hiring in Europe today?
sources.excerpt: Companies with frequent AI use are about 4% more likely to take on additional staff. Only 15% of firms that use AI cite reducing labour costs as a factor.

sources.title: The 2026 Global Intelligence Crisis
sources.excerpt: there is little evidence of AI disruption in labor market data as of today. In fact, the forward-looking components of our labor market tracking have improved and AI data center construction appears to be driving a pick-up in construction hiring.

sources.title: Challenger Report: February Cuts Plunge, YTD Hiring Falls 56%
sources.excerpt: So far in 2026, AI has been cited for 12,304 job cut announcements, or 8% of job cut plans. In 2025, companies referenced AI for 54,836 announced layoff plans, 5% of total cuts during the year.

sources.title: Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence
sources.excerpt: We find no systematic increase in unemployment for highly exposed workers since late 2022, though we find suggestive evidence that hiring of younger workers has slowed in exposed occupations

sources.title: Research on AI and the labor market is still in the first inning
sources.publisher: Peterson Institute for International Economics (Jed Kolko)
sources.excerpt: The evidence on how AI is affecting the labor market today is inconclusive, and claims about harmful impacts on particular groups of workers are premature. Initial evidence suggests that transitional disruption from AI to date is not outpacing recent technological changes.

sources.title: Why the ATM didn't kill bank teller jobs, but the iPhone did
sources.excerpt: I'm skeptical that simply slotting AI into human-shaped jobs will have the results people seem to expect... as long as we are in that regime, I expect disappointing productivity gains and relatively little real displacement.

sources.title: AI-fueled layoffs are rising, but a great divide is emerging
sources.excerpt: 89% of the respondents said they have no plans to cut staff or lay off workers because of AI. Just 3% said they have already cut staff, while 7% said they have plans to reduce their workforce within the next year.

sources.title: Artificial Intelligence, Productivity, and the Workforce: Evidence from Corporate Executives
sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta / Duke University (Baslandze et al.)
sources.excerpt: Survey of ~750 CFOs finds firm-size-and-sector-weighted aggregate employment is expected to decline by less than 0.4% due to AI in 2026, implying ~502K workers. 50% of firms report no AI job replacement. Large firms expect workforce reductions; small firms expect modest gains.

sources.title: See which jobs are most threatened by AI, and who may be able to adapt
sources.excerpt: Two points of general agreement stand out: There's no measurable evidence so far that AI is putting Americans as a whole out of work, economists say. And while the victims of past workplace automation were mostly factory and trade workers, it's white collar jobs that are first in line for AI shake-ups today.

sources.title: Same Storm, Different Boats: Generative AI and the Age Gradient in Hiring
sources.publisher: RATIO Institute / Örebro University (Lodefalk, Löthman, Koch, Engberg)
sources.excerpt: An event study documents an accelerating decline in employment of 22–25-year-olds in high-AI-exposure occupations, reaching 5.5 per cent by early 2025 relative to less exposed occupations within the same employers, while employment of workers over 50 rose by 1.3 per cent.

sources.title: Pascual Restrepo on AI, Automation, and the Future of Work
sources.publisher: Yale Department of Economics (Restrepo, interviewed by Strathmann)
sources.excerpt: A lot of these claims are premature. Many of the people making them have an interest in selling a product, so you have to take them with a grain of salt. Right now I would describe the labor market as more of a wait-and-see environment. You cannot automate everything tomorrow because we simply don't have enough computing power to do it.

sources.title: How Will AI Affect the US Labor Market?
sources.excerpt: If it takes place over a decade, Goldman Sachs Research expects to see a 0.6 percentage point increase in the unemployment rate.

sources.title: Evaluating the Impact of AI on the Labor Market: January/February CPS Update
sources.excerpt: The addition of the January and February 2026 CPS and the introduction of Anthropic's 'Observed Exposure' metrics do not suggest any substantial changes. Occupational dissimilarity, industry dissimilarity, and exposure and usage metrics all remain flat, lie within historical ranges, or continue along pre-existing trends.

sources.title: Tracking the Impact of AI on the Labor Market
sources.publisher: The Budget Lab at Yale (Gimbel, Kendall, Kulsakdinun)
sources.excerpt: The addition of the March 2026 CPS and the introduction of Anthropic's February usage metrics do not suggest any substantial changes. Occupational dissimilarity, industry dissimilarity, and our exposure and usage metrics all remain flat, lie within historical ranges, or continue along the trends they were already exhibiting. Currently, measures of exposure, automation, and augmentation show no sign of being related to changes in employment or unemployment.

sources.title: How Will AI-driven Automation Actually Affect Jobs?
sources.publisher: Substack (Alex Imas, Soumitra Shukla — U of Chicago Booth)
sources.excerpt: The workers at greatest risk are not necessarily those with the highest average exposure, but those whose jobs are built around a small number of core tasks that AI can automate.

sources.title: Weak Bundle, Strong Bundle: How AI Redraws Job Boundaries
sources.publisher: Garicano, Li & Wu (LSE / University of Hong Kong)
sources.excerpt: In weak-bundle occupations, AI automates some tasks and narrows the boundary of the job, leading to the standard task-substitution channel. In strong-bundle occupations where tasks are not independently reallocable, AI improves performance inside the job, but does not remove the human from the bundle.

sources.title: Will Wired Belts Become the New Rust Belts? AI and the Emerging Geography of American Job Risk
sources.publisher: Digital Planet, The Fletcher School, Tufts University
sources.excerpt: Industry-wide vulnerability to job displacement is approximately 6%... 9.3 million jobs are vulnerable to job loss due to AI under our median adoption path, with a plausible range of 2.7 to 19.5 million

sources.title: Where can AI be used? Insights from a deep ontology of work activities
sources.publisher: MIT Center for Collective Intelligence (Cai, YeckehZaare, Sun et al.)
sources.excerpt: 75% of AI application market value concentrated in software and information tasks. Physical work activities remain largely unaffected. Think/Do/Interact ontology of 39,603 activities based on O*NET 29.1.

sources.title: Mapping AI into Production: A Field Experiment on Firm Performance
sources.publisher: INSEAD / Harvard Business School (Kim, Kim, Koning)
sources.excerpt: Despite faster growth, treated firms do not scale inputs proportionally. Their demand for external capital investment falls by 39.5% relative to the control group, while their demand for labor remains unchanged.

sources.title: Forecasting the Economic Effects of AI
sources.publisher: Forecasting Research Institute (w/ Fed Chicago, Yale, Stanford, UPenn)
sources.excerpt: In a rapid AI progress scenario, economists forecast a drop in labor force participation from its 2025 baseline of 62.6% to 59.1% in 2030 and 55% in 2050, with roughly half of this decline—equivalent to 10 million jobs—attributable to AI.

sources.title: The Enterprise AI Playbook: Lessons from 51 Successful Deployments
sources.publisher: Stanford Digital Economy Lab (Pereira, Graylin, Brynjolfsson)
sources.excerpt: Headcount reduction was the largest outcome in 45% of the deployments, but alternatives (hiring avoided, redeployment, no reduction) accounted for 55%.

sources.title: Economists Once Dismissed the A.I. Job Threat, but Not Anymore
sources.excerpt: researchers at Boston Consulting Group estimated that more than half of the jobs in the United States would be 'reshaped' by artificial intelligence over the next two to three years but that far fewer would be replaced entirely.

sources.title: BLS Employment Situation: Total Nonfarm Payrolls — March 2026
sources.excerpt: Total nonfarm payrolls rose by 571K in March 2026 to 157,775K.

sources.title: BLS Unemployment Rate — March 2026
sources.excerpt: Unemployment rate 4.3% in March 2026, down 0.1 percentage points.

sources.title: Generative AI's Impact on Employment: Opportunities and Displacement Risks
sources.excerpt: The paper maps both the opportunities GenAI creates and the structural challenges it poses to workers across skill levels. It underscores the uneven distribution of risk, with routine cognitive roles facing the greatest exposure.

sources.title: Goldman Sachs on AI Agents and Labor Market Impact
sources.excerpt: Our analysis implies that AI substitution has reduced monthly payroll growth by roughly 25k and raised the unemployment rate by 0.16 percentage points over the past year, while augmentation has added about 9k to monthly payroll growth and lowered the unemployment rate by 0.06pp. This implies a net drag of 16k per month on payroll growth and a 0.1pp boost to the unemployment rate.

sources.title: JPMorgan Chase 2025 Annual Report — CEO Letter (Jamie Dimon)
sources.excerpt: AI will definitely eliminate some jobs, while it enhances others. There is a possibility that AI deployment will move faster than workforce adaptation to new job creation. In prior technological transformations, labor had time to adjust and retrain.

sources.title: Industrial Policy for the Intelligence Age: Ideas to Keep People First
sources.excerpt: If progress continues, we can expect systems to be capable of carrying out projects that currently take people months. This shift will reshape how organizations run, how knowledge is created, and how people find meaning and opportunity.

sources.title: AI and Coder Employment: Compiling the Evidence
sources.excerpt: They find that among 22-25 year olds employment in the top two quartiles of AI exposure fell about 12 percent relative to employment in the bottom quartile. Starting from total private employment of 130 million, and assuming about 7.6 percent of the workforce is 22-25 years old (based on the CPS), a 12 percent job loss for two quartiles works out to about 475,000 jobs lost.

sources.title: AI Blamed Heavily For March Job Cuts, Report Says
sources.excerpt: U.S.-based employers announced 60,620 job cuts in March, according to Challenger, up 25% from 48,307 cuts announced in February. AI was the leading reason for cutting jobs, cited in 25% of announcements, followed by closings, restructuring and economic conditions.

sources.title: AI's Tech Displacement Effect: Gen Z and the 16,000 Jobs-per-Month Drag
sources.excerpt: New research by Goldman Sachs economists finds that AI is already a measurable drag on the U.S. job market—erasing roughly 16,000 net jobs per month over the past year, with the pain falling hardest on Gen Z and entry-level workers. Goldman's breakdown shows AI substitution wiped out roughly 25,000 jobs per month in the past year, while augmentation added back about 9,000.

sources.title: Long-Term Effects of AI Job Losses
sources.excerpt: Recessions worsen outcomes: The effects of technology-related displacements are amplified (by three weeks of additional unemployment and a 5-percentage-point likelihood of subsequent joblessness). Goldman Sachs previously estimated that 6% to 7% of US workers (about 11 million people) could have their jobs displaced by AI.

sources.title: Use of Gen AI in the Workplace and the Value of Access to Training
sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of New York (Liberty Street Economics)
sources.excerpt: Around 62 percent of all respondents believe the unemployment rate will increase over the next twelve months due to AI, while around 11.6 percent expect it will decrease due to AI.

sources.title: The AI Jobs Transition Framework: Mapping AI's Near-Term Impact on Jobs
sources.excerpt: All 921 occupations (147.9M jobs): 18% of jobs are at a higher short-term automation risk; 46% of jobs are less likely to experience near-term change; 12% of jobs could grow because of AI; 24% of jobs may see declining employment as their task composition shifts, but the remaining jobs will still need workers. People that are or were employed in jobs we predict to have less immediate change have actually seen the largest increase in unemployment at +0.6 p.p. For comparison, people employed in jobs at higher automation risk or jobs that will reorganize have seen +0.3 p.p. and +0.3 p.p. increases in the unemployment rate over the same period.

sources.title: It's not 'bad marketing' from A.I. companies
sources.excerpt: What A.I. company executives are saying about their products — that they might lead to human extinction and almost certainly will lead to large-scale permanent disemployment — is so obviously 'bad messaging' that I would really urge people to consider that it's not a 'message' at all.

sources.title: Labor Automation Forecasting Hub
sources.publisher: Metaculus / Renaissance Philanthropy / Schultz Family Foundation
sources.excerpt: Overall employment is projected to fall 1.9% by 2030 and fall 3.4% by 2035 due to AI-driven displacement. Unemployment for new 4-year college graduates is projected to more than double to 12% by 2035.

sources.title: You're (not) hired: Artificial intelligence and early career hiring in the Quarterly Workforce Indicators
sources.excerpt: The overall reduction in hires fully explains a 15% decline in employment in the most AI-exposed industries since large language models became available, representing a loss of over 150,000 early career jobs.

sources.title: A Technology-Driven Productivity Regime Shift
sources.excerpt: Output growth slowed from 3.1% to 2.6% per year. But hours growth fell from 1.9% to just 0.7%. The result: productivity growth rose from 1.3% to 2.2%. There are no signs of a slowdown in 2025, and early 2026 job growth points to continued flat employment outside healthcare and social services.

sources.title: The Carlyle Compass: Software do we go now
sources.publisher: Carlyle (Jason Thomas, Head of Global Research & Investment Strategy)
sources.excerpt: Our proprietary survey of AI integration efforts finds that only 11% of management teams expect AI to replace existing software subscriptions. Far more expect the move to AI-centric architectures to reduce maintenance spending on legacy infrastructure, save on consulting fees, and increase the productivity of existing workers, reducing future headcount needs. Figure 4 (Carlyle Proprietary Survey, April 2026): Internal headcount cited as AI spending offset by 26% of respondents — the largest single category.

sources.title: Forecasting the Economic Effects of AI
sources.publisher: NBER (Karger, Kuusela, Abaluck, Bryan, Halperin, Jones, Murphy, Trammell, et al.)
sources.excerpt: Conditional on a 'rapid' AI progress scenario, in which AI systems surpass human performance on many cognitive and physical tasks, experts forecast substantial, though not historically unprecedented, economic shifts: annualized GDP growth rising to around 4% and the labor force participation rate falling from its current level of 62% to 55% by 2050, with roughly half of that decline—equivalent to around 10 million lost jobs—attributable to AI. The average economist assigned a 61.4% probability to moderate or rapid progress, but only 14.0% to the rapid scenario. Unconditional economic forecasts are close to historical trends: median GDP growth 2.5% for 2030, LFPR 61.0% for 2030 vs 62.6% in 2025.

sources.title: What 81,000 people told us about the economics of AI
sources.excerpt: One fifth of the respondents in our survey voiced concern about economic displacement. Respondents' perceived threat from AI was correlated with our own measure of observed exposure, which reflects the percentage of a job's tasks for which Claude is used.

sources.title: The task is not the job: A supply-side answer to Amodei and Imas
sources.excerpt: Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, went on Fox News and said that AI will eliminate up to half of all entry-level white-collar jobs within one to five years. He named finance, consulting, law, and tech... the argument that 'half of entry-level white-collar jobs be gone in five years' confuses task automation with the extinction of jobs.

sources.title: What Makes New Work Different from More Work?
sources.publisher: MIT Stone Center / NBER (Autor, Chin, Salomons, Seegmiller)
sources.excerpt: Between 2011-2023, 18% of US workers were employed in jobs introduced since 1970. New work differs from more jobs in existing occupations because it requires novel, scarce expertise, and therefore pays higher wages.

sources.title: How (un)Stable Are LLM Occupational Exposure Scores? Evidence from Multi-Model Replication
sources.excerpt: in a difference-in-differences framework, individual-level coefficient magnitudes vary 2.4-fold across annotators, and county level estimates flip from a significant negative to an insignificant positive depending on annotators
